children: A robust auction of 10-year U.S. Treasury notes
on Wednesday offered a welcome dose of afternoon relief to the bond market, helping to pare back an earlier surge in yields.
Before the auction, yields had jumped following a
by the Treasury Department detailing plans to significantly expand its next buyback of longer-dated bonds

. Following the afternoon sale, Treasury yields retraced some of those earlier gains as the market found its footing on the back of strong institutional demand, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising four basis points to 4.83% at press time, off around three bps from session highs.

Treasury sold $39B of the notes at a high yield of 4.834%, which was priced below what traders were anticipating heading into the bidding process, signaling robust investor appetite even as yields hover at elevated, multi-year levels.

The sale drew a highly competitive bid-to-cover ratio of 2.71, marking a notable jump compared with the 2.53 ratio seen during last month's $42B 10-year auction. Indirect bidders, a group that typically includes foreign central banks and international asset managers, drove much of this momentum by snapping up more than 79% of the notes, while direct bidders accounted for another 16.5%.

Because end-user demand was so strong, primary dealers—the large banks required to bid on and absorb any excess supply—were left taking down just over 4% of the auction. This was a far smaller portion than their recent historical average, confirming that the broader market easily digested the debt issuance on its own without needing the dealers to step in as buyers of last resort.

title: 10-year Treasury auction brings afternoon relief to bond market
